data.name: Sun
text:
Sun
Note: The Sun, our very own star, is a massive ball of hot plasma that sits at the center of our solar system.
It's the source of all life and energy on Earth, so I've colored it chlorophyll green in our plot!
* Type: A yellow dwarf star (G-type main-sequence star).
* Age: About 4.6 billion years old, and is expected to continue its current phase for about 5 billion years
more, then evolve into a Red Giant.
* Diameter: Roughly 1.4 million kilometers (865,000 miles), about 109 times the diameter of Earth.
* Mass: About 333,000 times the mass of Earth
* Composition: Primarily hydrogen (about 73%) and helium (about 25%), with trace amounts of other elements.
* Surface Temperature: 5778 K, around 5,500 degrees Celsius, or 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit
* Core Temperature: Around 15 million degrees Celsius (27 million degrees Fahrenheit)
* Stellar Class: Main-sequence. Stars in the prime of their lives, fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores.
* Absolute Magnitude: 4.83
* Spectral Type: G2V
* Object Type: Star
The Sun is composed of several layers:
* Core: The innermost region where nuclear fusion occurs, converting hydrogen into helium and releasing energy.
* Radiative Zone: Energy from the core travels outward through this zone via radiation.
* Convective Zone: Energy is transported through this zone via convection (the movement of hot plasma).
* Photosphere: The visible surface of the Sun.
* Chromosphere: A thin layer above the photosphere.
* Corona: The outermost layer, a very hot and tenuous plasma that extends millions of kilometers into space.
Standard for comparison to other stars:
* Luminosity: 1.000000 Lsun
* Mass: 1.00 Msun
* Distance: 0 pc (0 ly)
* Plotting marker size: 12 px

data.name: New Horizons Jupiter Gravity Assist
text:
New Horizons Jupiter Gravity Assist
Date: 2007-02-28 05:43:40 UTC
Distance: 0.01541 AU (2.31 million km)
Velocity relative to Jupiter: 21.22 km/s
Velocity relative to Sun: 23.00 km/s
Type: Gravity Assist

Fastest launch ever: 16.26 km/s Earth-relative,
combining with Earth's orbital velocity to ~43
km/s heliocentric (velocities add as vectors, not
scalars). The Sun's gravity steadily slowed it to
~19 km/s by Jupiter. The gravity assist added ~4
km/s, boosting speed to ~23 km/s -- partially
recovering what the Sun took. Without this boost,
Pluto arrival would have been three years later.

Source: NASA/JPL

data.name: New Horizons Pluto Flyby
text:
New Horizons Pluto Flyby
Date: 2015-07-14 11:49:57 UTC
Distance: 0.0000834 AU (12,472 km)
Velocity relative to Pluto: 13.78 km/s
Velocity relative to Sun: 14.52 km/s
Type: Flyby

First spacecraft to explore Pluto. Flew 12,472 km
above the surface at 13.78 km/s. Also passed
within 28,800 km of Charon. Revealed Pluto's
heart-shaped nitrogen ice plain (Sputnik Planitia)
and atmospheric haze layers.
Close-up trajectory fetched at 1-minute
resolution. Full mission trace (if visible) uses
coarser 6h steps and may diverge at this scale.

Source: NASA/JPL

data.name: New Horizons Arrokoth Flyby
text:
New Horizons Arrokoth Flyby
Date: 2019-01-01 05:33:22 UTC
Distance: 0.0000237 AU (3,538 km)
Velocity relative to Arrokoth: 14.43 km/s
Velocity relative to Sun: 13.87 km/s
Type: Flyby

Most distant planetary flyby in history at 43.4
AU from the Sun. Revealed a contact binary
"snowman" shape -- two lobes gently merged. First
close-up look at a pristine Kuiper Belt object,
offering clues to how planetesimals formed at the
dawn of the solar system.
Trajectory from SWRI NavSBE_2014MU69_od159
solution. Vectors only -- no osculating elements
available. Trajectory resolution set by adaptive
fetch step.

Source: NASA/JPL
